summary: KS3 learners (ages 11-13) move from calculating a single mean to describing and comparing whole distributions of one variable: computing mean, median, mode and range, judging which average best represents a data set given its shape, and reasoning about how an outlier affects each measure differently. Two judgements carry the topic: (1) the three averages are not interchangeable — the mean is pulled by every value (so an outlier drags it) while the median is robust, so the choice of average must fit the data's shape; and (2) an average alone does not describe a distribution — comparing two sets needs a measure of centre AND a measure of spread (range) together, because two sets with the same mean can differ widely in variability.
misconceptions: Reporting the mean as 'the average' regardless of skew or outliers, when the median would better represent a typical value
Thinking an outlier affects the mean and median equally, or deleting an outlier without justification, rather than seeing the mean is dragged while the median is robust
Comparing two data sets on their averages alone and ignoring the spread (a frequent error is to ignore variability entirely)
Giving the range as the two extreme values rather than their difference; or situating the mean at the centre of the range even when the data is skewed

activities.title: Watch the averages diverge: move a value far out
steps: Start with a small set of values on a stated scale (for example reaction times in whole seconds, or scores out of 40) clustered around 4-5, and compute the mean, median, mode and range by hand.
Record all four measures, then take ONE of those values and move it far out to a value the scale allows (for example 30), keeping the number of data points the same.
Recompute the mean and median with the far-out value, and compare each to its value before.
State in words which measure moved a lot and which barely moved, and explain why the mean was dragged while the median held.

If a draggable dot plot with mean, median, mode and range read out live is available, drag one point far from the cluster and watch the mean line chase it while the median stays put or moves at most to a neighbouring value in the cluster (for example, if the dragged point crosses from below the middle to above it) — this makes the differential effect visible in real time.
activities.insight: The mean is influenced by every value, so a single extreme value shifts it a lot; the median, based on order/position, is robust and barely moves. 'Robust' becomes concrete when you see the two measures respond differently to the same far-out value.

activities.title: Same mean, different spread: why centre is not enough
steps: Take two data sets (for example two classes' test scores) that have the same mean but clearly different spreads.
Compute the mean and the range (highest minus lowest, a single number) for each set.
Decide whether 'same mean' means the classes performed identically, and justify the answer using the ranges.
Write a conclusion in context that mentions BOTH centre and spread, e.g. 'Both classes scored about the same on average, but Class A was far more consistent.'
If side-by-side dot plots with adjustable spreads at a fixed mean are available, line the two plots up and compare how wide each is while the mean stays equal.
activities.insight: An average alone does not describe a distribution. Two sets with equal means can differ widely in variability, so a fair comparison reports a measure of centre AND a measure of spread.

activities.title: Which average would you report, and why?
steps: Given a skewed data set (or one with an outlier), compute mean, median and mode and note where each falls.
Choose which average best represents a typical value and write a one-sentence justification tied to the data's shape.
For a most-common / categorical question, decide whether the mode is the right choice and say why.
Check a tempting claim such as 'the mean always sits in the middle of the range' against your skewed data and explain whether it holds.
activities.insight: The appropriate average depends on the data: the median represents a typical value better for skewed data or data with an outlier; the mode suits most-common / categorical questions; the mean suits roughly symmetric numerical data. Learners' informal notions of 'average' (most frequent, reasonable value, midpoint, algorithm) are each true only in some circumstances.

activities.title: Compute-and-justify checks
steps: Compute mean, median, mode and range for a given set, stating the range as one number (highest − lowest).
For a skewed set, pick which average best represents it and give the reason.
For two sets, write a conclusion that cites BOTH an average AND the range, so a centre-only comparison is marked incomplete.
For an outlier item, state which of the mean or median changes more when the outlier is removed, and by roughly how much.

Optional: a usable worked set is sleep hours 7, 8, 8, 7, 9, 8, 2 (mean 7, median 8, mode 8, range 7), where the outlier 2 pulls the mean DOWN below the cluster — note this direction is opposite to an upward-pulling outlier, and the median stays representative.
activities.insight: Correct computation plus correct judgement (choice of average, differential outlier effect, centre-and-spread comparison) are both required; getting the arithmetic right is not the same as reasoning about the distribution.

checkQuestion: Give the child a small data set with a clear outlier — e.g. hours of sleep: 7, 8, 8, 7, 9, 8, 2 — and a second pair of data sets for comparison (two classes' test scores with similar means but different spreads). Set these tasks and WATCH how they work: (1) 'Find the mean, median, mode and range of the sleep data.' (2) 'Which average best describes a typical night's sleep here? Use it.' (3) 'Compare these two classes and tell me what you can conclude.' (Set the task and WATCH — do not hint that the 2 is an outlier, nor that comparing needs spread as well as an average.)
checkAnswer: A correct performance: computes mean, median, mode and range correctly (range = highest − lowest, one number); recognises the 2 as an outlier that drags the MEAN down while the MEDIAN stays representative, and reports the median as the typical value with that reason; and when comparing the two classes uses BOTH an average AND the range/spread ('similar on average but Class A is more consistent'), not the average alone. Seeing the outlier's differential effect and comparing on centre AND spread are the marks of mastery.
